## Ecclesiastes 2 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — *“I said to myself, ‘Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy what is good!’ But it proved to be futile.”*

**Traditional Reading:** Having tried wisdom in chapter 1 and found it wanting, Qoheleth now turns to pleasure as a possible source of life’s meaning. He addresses his own heart—the seat of emotions—and invites it to test *mirth* (gladness, enjoyment). The experiment is deliberate and controlled: he is testing pleasure, not abandoning himself to it thoughtlessly. The verdict, announced upfront, is that this too is *hebel*—futile, empty, like vapour.

- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** “Solomon tested the theory many live under today; that the meaning of life is found in more and varied pleasures, entertainments, and excitements.” He notes that “the Preacher is not testing pleasure so much as himself” (quoting Eaton).
- **Ellicott:** “Kohéleth, having tried wisdom and philosophic investigation, proceeded next to see what cheerful enjoyment could do for human happiness.” The address is “to mine heart” (cf. Luke 12:19).
- **Precept Austin:** Notes the NET translation: “Come now, I will try self-indulgent pleasure to see if it is worthwhile.” The key phrase is “to see what is good”—Qoheleth sought to discover whether merry-making offered any value to mankind. Ryrie summarises: Solomon’s pursuit of fulfilment through indulgence, achievements, possessions and fame “all failed to bring enduring satisfaction.”
- **Gill:** Solomon “proceeds to the experiment of pleasure, and tries whether any happiness was in that.” The pleasures in view are “manly, rational, and lawful pleasures,” not sordid lusts, since “he was guided and governed by his wisdom, and that remained in him” (v. 3).

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-2-commentary
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/2.htm (excerpts from search)

---

### v. 2 — *“I said of laughter, ‘It is folly,’ and of pleasure, ‘What does it accomplish?’”*

**Traditional Reading:** Solomon distinguishes between *laughter* (superficial gaiety, the “fun” of a party — Prov 10:23) and *mirth/pleasure* (more thoughtful joy). He dismisses laughter as “madness” and finds that pleasure accomplishes nothing of lasting value.

- **Guzik:** “Like a modern celebrity he ran from party to party, entertainment to entertainment. At the end of it all, he judged it to be ‘Madness’ and without accomplishment.” Eaton (quoted) says laughter is “a superficial gaiety” and mirth is “thoughtful pleasure.”
- **Ellicott:** Cross-references Proverbs 14:13 — “Even in laughter the heart may ache.”
- **Gill:** “As for that which at first sight was vain, frothy, and frolicsome, he dispatches at once, and condemns it as mad and unprofitable.”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/2.htm

---

### v. 3 — *“I sought to cheer my body with wine and to embrace folly—my mind still guiding me with wisdom—until I could see what was worthwhile for men to do under heaven during the few days of their lives.”*

**Traditional Reading:** Solomon experimented with wine and folly, but crucially *his mind was still guiding him with wisdom*. This was not unrestrained dissipation; it was a controlled experiment. The Hebrew word for “guiding” (Ellicott notes) is the word used of a shepherd or driver leading a flock (cf. 2 Sam 6:3; Ps 80:1).

- **Guzik:** “The Preacher lived a life satiated with the pleasures of wine and light, frivolous amusements. He wanted to see what was good for the sons of men to do if this life was all there was.”
- **Ellicott:** “Kohéleth contemplated not an unrestrained enjoyment of pleasure, but one controlled by prudence.” The phrase “all the days” (margin) is literally “for their span of life”—the few numbered days.
- **Gill:** Solomon tested “good eating and drinking, in a moderate way, without abuse.”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/2.htm

---

### vv. 4–8 — *“I expanded my pursuits. I built houses and planted vineyards… made gardens and parks… reservoirs… acquired menservants and maidservants… herds and flocks… silver and gold… male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men—many concubines.”*

**Traditional Reading:** These verses record Solomon’s vast building projects, agricultural enterprises, wealth, and pleasures. Commentators agree this is a catalogue of unparalleled achievement and acquisition. The word translated “concubines” (or “musical instruments” in some versions) is debated: the Hebrew *shiddah weshiddoth* occurs nowhere else.

- **Guzik:** “He tried to give life meaning through the satisfaction that comes through building and organizing and improving one’s environment.” Kidner is quoted: “As if he had over-reacted in turning to futile pleasures, he now gives himself to the joys of creativity.”
- **Ellicott:** “Parks” (v. 5) is the Persian word *pardes*, whence “paradise.” On v. 6, three gigantic reservoirs south of Bethlehem are still known as the “Pools of Solomon.” On v. 8, the “peculiar treasure of kings” refers to taxes and tribute. On the disputed final word of v. 8, Ellicott notes: “The interpretation ‘concubines’ is most in favour with commentators… it does appear unlikely that this notorious feature of Solomon’s court should be omitted.” But the traditional Jewish rendering is “musical instruments.” Both Guzik and Ellicott discuss the uncertainty.
- **Gill:** Enumerates “fine and spacious buildings; delightful vineyards, gardens, and orchards; parks, forests, and enclosures; fish pools, and fountains of water; a large retinue… immense riches… all kinds of music, vocal and instrumental.”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/2.htm

---

### v. 9 — *“So I became great and surpassed all in Jerusalem who had preceded me; and my wisdom remained with me.”*

**Traditional Reading:** Solomon’s greatness was genuine, and he maintained his capacity for objective assessment throughout the experiment. His wisdom “stood by” him (NASB) or “remained” with him.

- **Guzik:** “Solomon’s accomplishments rightly lifted him to prominence, and he had whatever meaning fame could bring to life.” He also emphasises that “in all of this Solomon did not lose his wisdom or ability to genuinely assess meaning and fulfillment.”
- **Ellicott:** “Kohéleth carried out his plan of tempering his enjoyment with discretion, but while he took his fill of the pleasure that fell to his lot, he found in it no abiding profit.”
- **Utley (StudyLight):** “All of these ‘things’ did provide a moment of joy and satisfaction, but it did not last!”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/ecclesiastes-2.html

---

### v. 10 — *“Anything my eyes desired, I did not deny myself. I refused my heart no pleasure. For my heart took delight in all my work, and this was the reward for all my labor.”*

**Traditional Reading:** Solomon exercised no restraint on his desires—he had the resources to satisfy every wish. He experienced real, though temporary, delight in his work. This delight, he says, was his *portion* (ḥēleq) or reward.

- **Guzik:** “We might say that the Preacher lived this period as a hedonist, but as an intelligent one. He looked for legitimate pleasures in life, such as the rightful pleasure one takes in the accomplishments of hard work.”
- **Precept Austin (quoting Eric Ortlund):** “In one sense, Qohelet’s second search succeeded because he was able to ‘look upon good’ … or ‘enjoy himself.’ Note that Qohelet remains within himself in v. 10, speaking of his own involvement in his work. This perspective changes in v. 11.”
- **Guzik (quoting Trapp):** “How many are there that have died of the wound in the eye!”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-2-commentary

---

### v. 11 — *“Yet when I considered all the works that my hands had accomplished and what I had toiled to achieve, I found everything to be futile, a pursuit of the wind; there was nothing to be gained under the sun.”*

**Traditional Reading:** When Solomon stepped back and considered his achievements objectively rather than experientially, his joy evaporated. Everything was *hebel* and *re‘ut ruach* (“striving after wind”). There was no *yitron* (lasting profit/advantage). This is the key conclusion of the first half of the chapter.

- **Guzik:** “Solomon examined his life lived for pleasure – even legitimate pleasures – and saw that it too was meaningless. All was vanity. There was no enduring, eternal sense of meaning.” He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: “This is as modern as ennui of every human soul which seeks knowledge, mirth, wealth, life – and forgets God.”
- **Utley:** This is “the question of how to find purpose in life without God; without God, life becomes just physical existence!”
- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary:** “All his achievements brought him a certain amount of satisfaction. But as he looks back he confesses that they brought him no nearer to solving the mystery of life’s purpose.”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/ecclesiastes-2.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ecclesiastes-2.html

---

### v. 12 — *“Then I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly; for what more can the king’s successor do than what has already been accomplished?”*

**Traditional Reading:** Having tested pleasure, Qoheleth returns to examine wisdom alongside madness and folly. The verse is grammatically difficult. Ellicott gives two interpretations: (1) “If the king has failed in his experiment, what likelihood is there that a private person should be more successful?” or (2) more simply, “the king’s successor can do no more than run the same round that has been trodden by his predecessor.” The latter connects with the theme that “there is nothing new under the sun.”

- **Ellicott:** Prefers the second reading, noting that “the theme of the whole section is that in human affairs there is no progress.”
- **Guzik:** “Solomon here spoke of himself as the son of David (Eccl 1:1); yet he also spoke of his own successor (who turned out to be Rehoboam, 1 Kings 11:43). Of both, Solomon understood that the new king can do only what he has already done.”
- **Expositor’s Bible Commentary (StudyLight / TEB):** “It is characteristic of the philosophic temper of our author… that, after pronouncing Wisdom and Mirth vanities… he does not at once proceed to try a new experiment, but pauses to compare these two ‘vanities,’ and to reason out his preference of one over the other.”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ecclesiastes-2.html

---

### vv. 13–14 — *“And I saw that wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness: The wise man has eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I also came to realize that one fate overcomes them both.”*

**Traditional Reading:** Wisdom does have genuine relative value—it is as superior to folly as light is to darkness. The wise person sees where he is going; the fool stumbles blindly. Yet this advantage is ultimately nullified by death, which claims both wise and foolish alike.

- **Ellicott:** “Wisdom surely has an advantage over folly, yet how full of ‘vanity’ is that advantage. Let the wise man have done his best, soon death comes; the wise man is forgotten.” The word for “excelleth” is the same “profit” (*yitron*) used in 1:3.
- **Guzik:** “No matter how wise one is or is not… the same event happens to them all: they all die.” Kidner is quoted: “Everything may tell us that wisdom is not on a par with folly, not goodness with evil; but no matter: if death is the end of the road, the contention that there is nothing to choose between them will get the last word.”
- **Expositor’s Bible Commentary:** “It is by the light of wisdom that he has learned the vanity of mirth, nay, the insufficiency of wisdom itself. But for that light he might still be pursuing pleasures which could not satisfy.”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ecclesiastes-2.html

---

### v. 15 — *“So I said to myself, ‘The fate of the fool will also befall me. What then have I gained by being wise?’ And I said to myself that this too is futile.”*

**Traditional Reading:** If the same death awaits both, what lasting advantage did all his wisdom bring? The question is rhetorical and despairing—under the “under the sun” premise, there is no answer.

- **Guzik:** “If death ends it all, then this life is robbed of true meaning. Even the good and great accomplishments of this world are unbelievably temporary, and therefore ultimately meaningless. The wise man dies just as the fool.”
- **Ellicott:** No separate comment beyond linking to the theme of the preceding verses.

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/

---

### v. 16 — *“For there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool, seeing that both will be forgotten in the days to come. Alas, the wise man will die just like the fool!”*

**Traditional Reading:** Not only do both die, but both are eventually forgotten. Even the memory of the wise fades. Ellicott notes that the original lacks a question mark after “wise man”—it should be read as an exclamation: “And how dies the wise man? As the fool!”

- **Ellicott:** “Better to omit the note of interrogation after ‘wise man,’ and put a note of exclamation after ‘fool,’ the ‘how’ being used as in Isaiah 14:4; Ezekiel 26:17.”
- **Ellicott also:** Raises the interesting point that if a later writer were composing this in Solomon’s name, “such a thought does not become a long subsequent writer who had been induced by Solomon’s reputation for wisdom to make him the hero of his work. It would seem to follow that the writer is here only giving the history of Solomon’s reflections, and not his ultimate conclusions.”

**Sources:**
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm

---

### v. 17 — *“So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me. For everything is futile and a pursuit of the wind.”*

**Traditional Reading:** Given the “under the sun” premise (life without eternity or God’s judgment in view), Solomon’s hatred of life is the logical conclusion. The Hebrew says literally “I hated lives” (plural)—possibly referring to all stages and conditions of life.

- **Guzik:** “Given his premise of life under the sun, Solomon hated life because it was so meaningless.” He quotes Clarke: “The lives, both of the wise, the madman, and the fool. Also all the stages of life… There was nothing in it worth pursuing, no period worth re-living.”
- **Kidner (quoted by Guzik):** “If there is a lie at the centre of existence, and nonsense at the end of it, who has the heart to make anything of it?”
- **Desiring God (John Piper):** Quotes Eccl 2:17–18 as part of the Preacher’s realism: “Yet even in the midst of it, he could still call people to rejoice always in the pleasures of life and to do so recognizing them as a gift of God.”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ecclesiastes-finding-joy-amidst-lifes-enigmas

---

### vv. 18–19 — *“I hated all for which I had toiled under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me. And who knows whether that man will be wise or foolish? Yet he will take over all the labor at which I have worked skillfully under the sun. This too is futile.”*

**Traditional Reading:** Death not only ends life but also forces the transfer of all one’s accomplishments to a successor who may be a fool. Solomon’s own successor was Rehoboam, whose foolishness split the kingdom (1 Kings 12).

- **Guzik:** “This concern was well founded, because after Solomon’s death, Rehoboam turned out to be a fool in many ways.” He quotes Clarke: “Alas! Solomon, the wisest of all men, made the worst use of his wisdom, had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and yet left but one son behind him… and that one was the silliest of fools!”
- **Ellicott:** “There seems to be no special reference to Rehoboam, but only the assertion of the general principle that the wisest of men must leave all that his labour has gained to be enjoyed by another who may be destitute of wisdom.”
- **Guzik (Eaton):** “The only conclusion is that it is all useless. An abyss of despair results. He ‘allowed [his] heart to despair’… This is one of the most moving points of the Old Testament, the antithesis of the New Testament’s ‘not in vain in the Lord’ (1 Corinthians 15:58).”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm

---

### v. 20 — *“So my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun.”*

**Traditional Reading:** The Hebrew verb suggests “turned to despair” or “allowed the heart to despair.” This is a deliberate turning—a reasoned surrender to hopelessness under the “under the sun” logic.

- **Ellicott:** “Went about” (KJV) — the same verb as in Eccl 7:25; 9:14; 12:5.
- **Guzik:** See v. 18 notes above for Eaton’s comment on this despair.

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm

---

### v. 21 — *“When there is a man who has labored with wisdom, knowledge, and skill, and he must give his portion to a man who has not worked for it, this too is futile and a great evil.”*

**Traditional Reading:** The injustice is acute: a person works with wisdom, knowledge, and *skill* (Ellicott: “equity” in KJV, but better “skill, success”), yet must leave everything to someone who did nothing to earn it. This is not merely futile—it is a “great evil” (*rabbah ra‘ah*).

- **Ellicott:** “Equity.—Rather, skill, success (Eccl 4:4; 5:7). The noun is peculiar to this book.”
- **Guzik:** Sees this as part of death’s defeat of all accomplishments.

**Sources:**
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/

---

### vv. 22–23 — *“For what does a man get for all the toil and striving with which he labors under the sun? Indeed, all his days are filled with grief, and his task is sorrowful; even at night, his mind does not rest. This too is futile.”*

**Traditional Reading:** Work brings grief, sorrow, and sleeplessness—and for what? The rhetorical question expects the answer: nothing of lasting value.

- **Ellicott:** “The fact that the wise man must surrender his acquisitions exhibits the inutility of the painful toil by which he has gained them.”
- **Guzik:** If death robs work of meaning, “life is indeed sorrowful, work is burdensome, and there is no rest or relief from the despair of a meaningless life.” He notes that the Preacher hints at a vital question: *why does this bother us so much?* Humans are not designed merely for temporal existence; the discontent itself points toward eternity (anticipating 3:11).
- **Kidner (quoted by Guzik):** “Incidentally, this bitter reaction is a witness to our ability to stand clear of our condition and to weigh it up. To be outraged at what is universal and unavoidable suggests something of a divine discontentment, and hint of what the great saying in Ecclesiastes 3:11 will call ‘eternity’ in man’s mind.”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm

---

### v. 24 — *“Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. I have also seen that this is from the hand of God.”*

**Traditional Reading:** This is the first of several “carpe diem” passages in Ecclesiastes (see also 3:12–13, 22; 5:18–20; 8:15; 9:7–10). Under the “under the sun” premise, the best one can do is find contentment in simple, everyday pleasures: eating, drinking, and taking satisfaction in work. Yet these are not autonomous—they are “from the hand of God.”

- **Guzik:** “It seems that the Preacher advised us how to make the best of a bad situation. If life really is as despairing and meaningless as he has shown it to be, then we should simply accept that true meaning is impossible to find, and simply find contentment in moderate and responsible pleasures.” He adds: “This thinking may work in making a bad situation better; but it gives no true meaning to life in light of eternity.” He quotes Trapp: “This may seem to savor of epicurism… For which cause some of the old Jew doctors were once in a mind to hide this whole book out of the way.”
- **Ellicott:** Notes a textual issue: “Nothing better.—‘Not good’ is the sense of the Hebrew as it stands, for… the word ‘than’ is in italics.” If the text is not emended, the sense is “It is not good for a man to eat, etc., seeing it depends on God whether or not that is possible.” But most interpreters agree with the traditional reading (“nothing is better than…”).
- **Ligonier (Reformed):** On the related theme in Eccl 5:18ff, “the Preacher commends finding joy not only in one’s financial success but in the very work that leads to that prosperity. It is a good thing to find enjoyment in our toil… Work is not an evil to be avoided but a gift from the Lord to be embraced.”
- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary:** “God intends people to enjoy the good things of life and to find enjoyment in their work. This is God’s gift.”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/enjoyment-our-toil
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ecclesiastes-2.html

---

### v. 25 — *“For apart from Him, who can eat and who can find enjoyment?”*

**Traditional Reading:** Ellicott notes a significant textual variant. The KJV reads “more than I,” but the Septuagint (LXX) and many modern versions read “without Him” (as the BSB does). The sense is that genuine enjoyment of life’s simple pleasures is impossible apart from God’s enabling.

- **Ellicott:** “There is a various rendering, which has the authority of the LXX, and which has every appearance of being right: ‘without Him.’”
- **Guzik:** In his NKJV-based commentary, the verse is rendered “For who can eat, or who can have enjoyment, more than I?” He explains: given the Preacher’s premise, his life should be the best in a meaningless world—yet “his life was almost infinitely poorer than the most humble life lived with true meaning.”

**Sources:**
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/

---

### v. 26 — *“To the man who is pleasing in His sight, He gives wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner He assigns the task of gathering and accumulating that which he will hand over to one who pleases God. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.”*

**Traditional Reading:** God’s sovereign distribution is stated: the one who pleases Him receives wisdom, knowledge, and joy; the sinner merely gathers wealth that will ultimately be transferred to the righteous. Yet even this apparent divine justice is declared “vanity and grasping for the wind”—because from an “under the sun” perspective, it offers no ultimate satisfaction.

- **Guzik:** “Solomon reflected on how sometimes it seems that what the sinner has gathered and collected is given to him who is good before God. This might seem unjust, but even under the sun, sometimes injustice seems to work in one’s favor.” He quotes Kidner: “The fact that in the end the sinner’s hoard will go to the righteous is only a crowning irony to what was in any case vanity and a striving after the wind.”
- **Ellicott:** “On the doctrine that the wicked amass wealth for the righteous, see marginal references” (e.g., Prov 13:22; Job 27:16–17).
- **Expositor’s Bible Commentary:** “This, whatever appearances may sometimes suggest, is the law of God’s giving: that the good shall have abundance, while the bad lack; that more shall be given to him who has wisdom to use what he has aright… Nevertheless even this wise use and enjoyment of temporal good does not and cannot satisfy the craving heart of man.”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-2/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/2.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ecclesiastes-2.html

## Where Traditions Differ

I was unable to access specific denominational pages (Baptist from gty.org, Methodist from seedbed.com, Lutheran from 1517.org or lcms.org, Pentecostal distinctives beyond enduringword.com) due to search/fetch limits. However, from the material I did obtain, here are the observable points of difference:

- **Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasises that the enjoyment of work is a *creational gift* not an evil, that work was given before the Fall, and that doing work “as for the Lord” (Col 3:23) transforms drudgery into delight. The Ligonier devotional explicitly corrects a “prevailing attitude… that says work is pure drudgery.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/enjoyment-our-toil)
- **Baptist / John Piper (Desiring God):** Piper reads Ecclesiastes as fuel for “stoking fires of joy in my soul.” He interprets *hebel* not primarily as “meaningless” but as “enigmatic” or “breath”—life is mysterious, not absurd. The Preacher is a “Preacher of Joy,” calling people to “God-conscious joy” amid life’s enigmas. Piper’s emphasis on joy as a commanded pursuit within the mystery stands somewhat distinct from the more pessimistic reading in Guzik. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ecclesiastes-finding-joy-amidst-lifes-enigmas)
- **Guzik (broadly Evangelical / Charismatic via Enduring Word):** Stresses that the Preacher’s despair comes specifically from “viewing life ‘under the sun’ without eternity.” His application is that “if we live as if eternity and God do not matter, we will end up exactly where Solomon did.” The enjoyment passages are seen as making “the best of a bad situation” rather than as positive divine commands.

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (netbible.org notes)

From the search excerpts, the NET Bible notes (referenced on Precept Austin) provide technical philological detail on key terms:
- **“Come now”** (v. 1): The Hebrew *lékhah* is a “weakened imperative, used merely as an introductory word” (cf. Gen 19:32; Judg 19:11). It functions “as an invitation to the audience to adopt a course of action that will be beneficial.”
- **“Test”** (*nasah*): Means “to conduct an experiment” (Judg 6:39; Dan 1:12, 14). Qoheleth is testing pleasure, not being tested by it.
- **“Futility”** (*hebel*): Denotes “futile, worthless, fruitless, pointless,” a synonym of “folly” in v. 2a and an antonym of *tov* (“worthwhile, beneficial”).
- **“See what is good”**: The volitive sequence (cohortative + imperative) denotes purpose/result: “I will test you… in order to see…”
- **“Heart”** (*leb*): A synecdoche for the whole person — “I said to myself.”

(Source: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-2-commentary, quoting NET notes)

### Older Critical Commentaries (Expositor’s Bible, via StudyLight)

The Expositor’s Bible Commentary gives a “philosophic” reading: Qoheleth pauses to compare wisdom and mirth *as vanities*, preferring wisdom because it is a light—it enabled him to *see* the vanity of mirth. Yet wisdom cannot explain why the same fate befalls both, nor why the labourer must leave his gains to an unworthy heir. The conclusion of the “First Act” is negative—two avenues (wisdom and pleasure) are closed off, but the search continues. “All we have learned is that one or two avenues along which we urge the quest will not lead us to the end we seek.”

(Source: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ecclesiastes-2.html)
